name: Face slimming/tightening mask (Rubinstein school)

card.summary: A 1940s salon contraption mask associated with beauty-school training, marketed for slimming and tightening the face through heat, pressure or electrical stimulation.
card.note: Historical device type; electrical and heated salon devices were later regulated differently.

quick.overview:
Mid-century beauty salons used contraptions fitted over or pressed to the face, aimed at firming sagging contours and slimming the face. One such device is pictured in 1940s images tied to a Helena Rubinstein beauty school.

The appearance goal was a tighter jawline and slimmer cheeks. Related devices such as Rubinstein's heated facial iron and Elizabeth Arden's diathermy masks promised improved circulation and contour; commentators of the time and later writers did not find corroboration for lasting change.
quick.how: These were salon treatments given by trained staff in courses of visits, often with creams or oils. Heat or electrical current was applied through the device while the client lay still.
quick.risks: Heat and electrical devices carry burn and irritation risks if misused. No risk data exist for this specific device; this is a historical technique.

lead: Beauty salons of the 1930s and 1940s used apparatus masks and irons intended to tighten and slim the face. A 1940s contraption mask linked to a Helena Rubinstein beauty school is described in retrospective photo captions as a slimming/tightening device.

Documented relatives show how the idea worked. Rubinstein introduced a Skin-Pressing Treatment in her Paris salon in the late 1940s using an electrically heated facial iron with her Huile Vitale oil, aimed at sagging contours [1]. Elizabeth Arden's Vienna Youth Mask, introduced 1927-28, used a face-moulded mask connected to a diathermy machine and was advertised as firming tissues without surgery [2].
The appearance payoff claimed was a firmer, slimmer, rosier face from improved circulation. Reviewers noted that heat can temporarily dilate vessels and plump the skin [1].

chain: Mask applies heat, pressure or current
Face looks firmer and slimmer, as marketed
angle.text: Salon clients used these devices hoping for a tighter, slimmer face. Any visible change would be short-lived skin plumping from heat and circulation.

paras: Facial irons were hand-held, often heated devices rolled over the face; makers claimed they smoothed wrinkles and improved contour, and Varady's was patented in 1931 [1]. Rubinstein's Skin-Pressing Treatment combined an electric iron with a hormone-containing oil, and a 1946 advertisement said heat and pressure drove oil deep into tissues [1].

Arden's Vienna Youth Mask was moulded to the face, at first plaster and later tinfoil-lined papier-mache, and wired to a diathermy machine; a course was about 32 treatments [2]. Arden dropped it in 1938 [2]. A 1935 New Yorker profile said medicine offered no corroboration for her theory, while agreeing that diathermy stimulates circulation [2].

timeline.event: Arden introduces the Vienna Youth Mask in London and Paris [2].
